text: I’ll model the finite oil region as the cylindrical space inside the ring bore (`r ≤ 23 mm`, `|z| ≤ 5 mm`) minus the spinner material. Thus the bore, radial clearance, and both 1 mm end gaps form one connected volume. The two open end cross-sections will be treated as separate ring-end patches; this is the necessary closure assumption for a finite CFD region. I’ll use a conformal Gmsh tetrahedral mesh after exporting the four CAD-derived patch STLs. First I’m building and measuring the coarse CAD volume.

The first measurement exposed a placement error: this build123d `Cylinder` is already centred axially, so my added translation shifted both solids downward. I’m correcting that explicitly and rendering a clipped view of the connected oil volume before proceeding.

The corrected CAD is one solid oil region with the requested dimensions. I’ll now inspect its seven exact boundary faces by surface type and area, which lets me map the CAD faces to patches without relying on bounding-box position heuristics.

The areas identify the patches unambiguously: the `r=23 mm` cylinder is the outer-ring wetted wall; the `r=22 mm`, `r=15 mm`, and two `z=±4 mm` annuli together are the spinner-wetted patch; the two `z=±5 mm` circular closures are the separately named end patches. I’ll export all four in one conformal tessellation call so their shared seams remain welded.

The patch export is closed and consistently wound (1,508 triangles, zero open/non-manifold/flipped edges). For volume meshing I’ll import the exact CAD fluid solid into Gmsh via STEP, then map its imported surfaces by exact surface area and centre of mass to the already established patch identities. This avoids meshing the faceted STL approximation.

The imported STEP preserves all seven CAD faces and their measured areas exactly. I’ll generate a deliberately coarse first volume mesh with a nominal 0.50 mm tetrahedral size—two elements across each 1 mm clearance—and retain the four requested surface groups plus an `oil` cell zone.
The coarse CAD-conformal mesh completed with about 354k exported tetrahedra. I’ll convert it to OpenFOAM format and inspect the resulting boundary names and face counts before running mesh checks.

Conversion produced exactly the four requested OpenFOAM patches and 354,287 tetrahedral cells; the converter’s temporary “undefined faces” warning is its normal pre-mapping stage, and all such faces were subsequently assigned (no `defaultFaces` patch remains). I’ll now run the binding bare `checkMesh`.

`checkMesh` did not reach the mesh because OpenFOAM 2512 requires placeholder `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries even for this utility. I’ll add only those required case dictionaries and rerun the same bare check.
The utility additionally parses the standard scheme subdictionaries. I’ll provide a complete minimal `fvSchemes` structure (still no solver setup or boundary conditions) and rerun the check.

The binding check passes: one connected region, correct `46 × 46 × 10 mm` bounds, volume within 0.01% of CAD, maximum aspect ratio 7.32, non-orthogonality 66.7°, and skewness 0.927. I’ll make one final cutaway rendering of the actual OpenFOAM mesh to visually confirm that cells occupy the bore, radial clearance, and both end gaps.

The isometric cutaway confirms the converted mesh exists, but its viewing angle hides the narrow internal channels. I’ll render the same clipped mesh normal to the cut plane so the two 1 mm clearances are directly visible.

The actual OpenFOAM mesh has been inspected in cutaway and cross-section. The finite-domain closure assumption is that the oil’s two circular end cross-sections at `z=±5 mm` are the separately named `ring_top_end` and `ring_bottom_end` patches; no external oil bath was added because no external domain dimensions were specified. A snappyHexMesh `locationInMesh` point is intentionally absent because this is a direct CAD-conformal Gmsh volume mesh.
